stories.headline: Hunted to under 1,000, giant tortoises now outnumber people
stories.summary: 19th-century hunting left fewer than 1,000 tortoises on Aldabra. After decades of protection, a new count estimates about 183,000 grown tortoises, more than the Seychelles' whole human population.
stories.why: Proof that protecting a place for decades can bring a species all the way back.

stories.headline: Neanderthals carved a wooden club unlike anything ever found
stories.summary: A rock shelter near Barcelona kept the hollow shapes of Neanderthal wooden tools: spears up to 2.45 m long, bark trays and a club with no clear match in prehistory, from 62,000 to 40,000 years ago.
stories.why: Wood almost never survives, so this shows a hidden side of Neanderthal skill.

stories.stat_label: of the world's heaviest insects freed
stories.headline: 11,000 of the world's heaviest insects are back in the wild
stories.summary: Wētāpunga, giant wētā as heavy as a mouse, once clung on to a single island. A 15-year breeding effort released 11,000 onto 8 predator-free islands and 2 sanctuaries, and they now breed there.
stories.why: The species went from Nationally Endangered to Nationally Increasing.

stories.stat_label: weeks for bleached coral to recover
stories.headline: Bleached corals fully recovered after touching a healthy twin
stories.summary: Stanford researchers placed bleached coral against a healthy clone of itself. Their tissues fused, the healthy one shared its algae, and the bleached coral fully recovered in just 7 weeks.
stories.why: Bleached corals aren't always a lost cause, a clue for future reef rescue.

fun_fact: Aldabra giant tortoises are among the largest tortoises in the world.
